title: Two People Remember Audrey Hepburn. Only One Can Be Right.
title_alternatives: Two People Remember Audrey Hepburn. Only One Can Be Right.
Twenty Minutes in One Room. Two Accounts. Both Impossible.
She Said Nothing to Anybody. She Also Said Goodbye by Name.
The Child Held Up a Notebook. Nobody Agrees What Happened.
Both Witnesses Were Honest. Their Accounts Cannot Both Be True.
description:
On a wet Thursday afternoon in October 1966, a hired car with a broken fan belt was pushed into a garage in a village in County Wicklow, and the woman travelling in it crossed the road to wait in the post office, because the garage had no heating and the post office had a stove.

She was there for twenty minutes.

Those twenty minutes were described in print twice. Once in 1970, by a man of thirty-eight, to a reporter from a county paper. And once in 1992, by a woman of forty-five, in a long interview recorded for a local history project.

The two accounts agree about the weather, the fan belt, the stove, the time of day, how long the wait lasted and who fixed the car. Past that point they agree about nothing at all.

In one of them she stands at the window for twenty minutes with her back to the room and speaks to nobody, and when a small girl holds up a notebook she says something short and turns back to the window.

In the other she spends most of the twenty minutes on a bench beside a confused woman of eighty-four, listening to a long story about a shop in Dublin that closed in 1938, and when the car is ready she goes round the room saying goodbye to four people, one of them by name.

These are not two angles on one event. They are two different events. Both witnesses were, by every test anybody has been able to apply, telling the truth as they remembered it.

The notebook survives. It ought to settle the question and it does the opposite.

There is exactly one detail both of them mention and neither of them thought was worth anything, and it is the only thing in the room that says the same thing in both accounts.

This story is a work of fiction. The village, the post office, Doyle, the Hanlons, the Byrnes, the notebook and every detail in it are invented, created for storytelling and not drawn from any record.
